title.narrative: Output 7.5. Increased capacity of constituents to develop fair and effective labour migration frameworks, institutions and services to protect migrant workers

description.narrative:
On 1 April 2020 the Foreigners' Work Management Policy Sub-committee of the Ministry of Labour endorsed the "Announcement on the list of prohibited occupations for employment of migrant workers". This list was revised and additional occupations were added to better reflect the employment of migrant workers in Thailand. Migrant workers can now also seek employment in construction (brickwork) and services sectors (shop keeping). This announcement offers additional protection to migrant workers as it formalises their employment in sectors with high prevalence of irregular migration and abusive practices.
The Ministry of Labour Department of Skills Development update its skills development curriculum to include the chapter on gender equality and green jobs. This contributes to stronger institutional mechanism to protect rights of migrant workers, especially women.
The Ministry of Labour has updated the training curriculum for labour inspectors to include a module on violence and harassment in the world of work and domestic workers rights. This will contribute to strengthening the role of the labour inspectors The ILO, with support of the Government of Australia and Canada, participated in the tripartite commission on migration management policy to discuss and finalize the list of prohibited occupations for employment of migrant workers. At the meeting, the Foreigners' Work Management Policy Sub-committee endorsed the draft Announcement, which would enter into force by the end of the Q3 2020. ILO has continuously advocated for the reduction of prohibitions in line with labour shortages and ground realities by participation in the meetings of the Sub-committee and through the representation at the Migrant Working Group (MWG)
ILO with support from the European Union, provided technical support to update the skill development curriculum to include the chapter on gender equality and green jobs.
The ILO also with support from the European Union revised the curriculum for training of labour inspectors to include module on violence and harassment in the world of work, domestic workers rights. This will contribute to strengthening the role of the labour inspectors. The ILO is also conducting the capacity training for 300 labour inspectors

Output 1.3. Increased institutional capacity of labour administrations

description.narrative:
The Ministry of Labour's Department of Labour Protection and Welfare (DLPW) revised its labour inspection guidelines to add sections on violence and harassment in the world of work, domestic work and forced labour with a focus on women migrant workers. The purpose was to improve the quality and effectiveness of labour inspection services on these priority compliance issues while improving labour protection coverage for vulnerable migrant women workers. This was followed up by the implementation of a training plan whereby the DLPW together with the ILO trained over 250 labour inspectors on the new guidelines (August – October 2021). The target labour inspectors were those with less than five years of experience and who work in provinces where migrant workers, particularly women, work and reside.
Representatives from the Thai Ministry of Labour, labour attachés from Myanmar and Cambodia, trade unions, civil society partners, and migrant workers representatives were brought together to share knowledge, experiences and good practices in addressing migrant workers' needs through enhanced border cooperation through labour attachés. The workshop increased inter-institutional understanding on the respective roles of labour attachés and consular officers in assisting migrant workers. Furthermore, the labour attachés increased their ability to provide quality services and advice to employers and workers on relevant labour laws, policies and policy changes, and complaint mechanisms in Thailand for migrant workers. This contributes to addressing the persistent decent work deficits of vulnerable and hard to reach migrant workers in the country. With support from the EU-UN Spotlight Initiative, ILO provided technical support in the revision of the labour inspection guidelines and subsequent training. These were also carried out in collaboration with the Thailand Development Research Institute (TDRI).
With support from Government of Australia and Canada, the ILO convened and led the workshop on enhancing cross-border cooperation for the protection of migrant workers with labour attachés, trade union and employer representatives, and key civil society partners in Thailand.

description.narrative:
To increase migrant workers' access to justice in Thailand, in 2016 the Ministry of Labour established Migrant Workers Assistance Centers (MWAC) in ten provinces throughout the country. In line with an assessment conducted in 2020, the Department of Employment developed standard operating procedures on collaboration and coordination with relevant bodies on case referral and case management for MWACs.
The Foundation for Labour and Employment Promotion (Homenet Thailand) and the Network of Domestic Workers in Thailand, are providing new services to migrant workers, including conducting empowerment activities to 9,725 women domestic workers in Thailand
The State Enterprises Workers' Relations Confederation (SERC), Raks Thai and the government run shelter in Thailand enhanced their support services (e.g. shelter, counselling, organizing, training, community outreach, case management) to migrant workers, with specific services for women migrant workers. They s mainstreamed strategies that look into issues of gender, violence against women, violence, harassment and trafficking). As a result, in 2020-2021 , these organizations provided services to 1,918 (1,237 women) migrant workers and their families. In 2020, the ILO, with support of the Government of Canada and Australia, launched a report entitled Ensuring migrant workers access to justice: An assessment of Thailand's Migrant Workers Assistance Centers. The report was made upon a request from the Ministry of Labour, and aims to holistically review the Migrant Workers Assistance Center model and provide recommendations on how to enhance the centres' effectiveness in delivering services to migrant workers. During the biennium, the ILO continued to support the MOL (DOE) to implement the recommendations by the 2020 assessment. In line with the recommendations, the ILO supported the DOE to develop standard operating procedures on collaboration and coordination with relevant bodies on case referral and case management for MWACs. Additionally, the assessment was published and disseminated to practitioners particularly officials at MWACs in ten provinces across Thailand.
Throughout the period, the ILO, with support of the Government of Canada and Australia, has been building the capacity of the Labour and Employment Promotion (Homenet Thailand) to be able to better advocate for increased labour protections for domestic workers, including migrant domestic workers, in Thailand, and to provide targeted services to this group of highly vulnerable workers.
With the support of the European Union, the ILO has provided technical assistance to State Enterprises Workers Relations Confederation (SERC), Raks Thai Foundation and two government run shelters (in Surat Thani and Nonthaburi) to provide direct assistance to migrant workers and their families. ILO supports the provision of specific services for women migrant workers, as well as mainstream services that look into issues of gender, violence against women, violence and harassment into the regular programming of local service providers. The shelters target victims of trafficking and children.
